name: Kusaghe, dialect of Hoava-Kusaghe
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Davis, Karen. 2003. A grammar of the Hoava language, Western Solomons. Pacific Linguistics 535. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU. xvi+332 pp. doi:10.15144/PL-535
catalog_locator: Scope: ch.3 intro p.23; dialect status sec. 2.1 pp. 8-10 and p.22. Stress: sec. 3.4.1-3.4.3 pp. 29-31. Intonation: sec. 3.5 p.31. Vowels: sec. 3.1.2 p.25.
catalog_quote: In this chapter I outline the phoneme system of Hoava, including the dialectal differences of Kusaghe ... [3.4.1] Two- and three-syllable underived words are stressed on the first syllable, as shown in the next examples: /híkɛ/ 'three'; /βɛ́lu/ 'yesterday'; /búlɔ/ 'heart' /máŋini/ 'warm' /kábasa/ 'house' /ámina/ 'Amina' Four-syllable underived words receive secondary stress on the first syllable and main stress on the third syllable: /ɣɔ̀lɔɣáɔ/ 'vine sp.'; /lìʤaβɛ́ti/ 'Elizabeth' [3.4.2] Words derived by reduplication retain main stress on the base of the word ... A regular stress shift occurs when a verb becomes transitive. The main stress shifts to the vowel immediately preceding the object marker: /hápu/ 'cover' /hapú-a/ 'cover-it' /hapu-í-ɣɔ/ 'cover-TR-you' ... the only marker of transitivity and object marking is the stress on the final vowel: /ŋáni/ 'eat' /ŋaní/ 'eat them' ... Movement of stress also occurs when some suffixes are added on to a word. The main stress moves to the syllable immediately preceding the suffix ... Derivational prefixes do not affect the placement of stress, which remains on the root of a word. [3.5] The Hoava, Kusaghe and Njela dialects differ in their intonation ... Both Kusaghe and Njela may lengthen the final stressed syllable of a phrase and sharply lower the pitch on that syllable, followed by a monotone for any remaining unstressed syllables: KUS /rá:ɔ ga ba si/ 'It's just me.'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (348 pp., text present; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A grammar of the Hoava language, Western Solomons', author Karen Davis; present listing sealang PL-535 provenance). Extracted pp. 39, 45-47 (printed pp. 23, 29-31) with extracted text. Every stitched piece of the reported quote is present at the stated locators: p.23 'In this chapter I outline the phoneme system of Hoava, including the dialectal differences of Kusaghe'; 3.4.1 p.29 'Two- and three-syllable underived words are stressed on the first syllable' (text renders the fi-ligature as 'flrst', a scan artefact only) and 'Four-syllable underived words receive secondary stress on the first syllable and main stress on…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Hoava-Kusaghe (Kusaghe treated as a dialect, differences noted where they exist): underived words of 1-3 syllables carry main stress on the first syllable; 4-syllable underived words have secondary stress on syllable 1 and main stress on syllable 3. In derived words placement is morphologically governed: reduplication, (-)in- nominalisation and derivational prefixes (ta-, va-, vari-) leave main stress on the root/base; nominaliser -ana is stressed on its own first syllable; transitive/object suffixes and suffixes such as -gu, -na, emphatic, vocative pull main stress to the syllable immediately preceding the suffix, and with a zero 3PL object marker final-vowel stress is the only exponent of transitivity. Kusaghe (and Njela) are reported to differ from Hoava only in phrase-final intonation (lengthening and pitch drop on the last stressed syllable of a phrase), not in word-stress placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four-syllable underived words: secondary stress on the first syllable, main stress on the third (p.29). Nothing stated for 5+ syllable underived words.
new_statements.exceptions: 3.4.3 Lexical stress (pp. 30-31): a few pairs distinguished only by stress, mostly where a derived word's root has been lost (e.g. 'banyan tree' vs 'desire', 'kite' vs 'back of canoe'); one genuine minimal pair hike 'three' vs hike 'three days ago', which Davis hedges as possibly an exaggerated citation-form difference. No Kusaghe-specific exceptions to word-stress placement are given; Kusaghe differences listed are segmental ([z] for Hoava [dʒ], stronger trill, less vowel elision, retention of /ɣ/) and intonational.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules (sec. 3.4) stated on citation/underived and derived words; phrase-level prominence handled separately in 3.5, where the Kusaghe/Njela trait is lengthening + pitch lowering of 'the final stressed syllable of a phrase' (example (33) is a Kusaghe utterance). Vowel length is not phonemic ('vowels can be lengthened when stressed', p.25; 'Kusaghe uses the same set of vowels').
new_statements.identity_note: The only description is Davis 2003, a grammar of 'Hoava-Kusaghe' that treats Hoava (hoav1238), Kusaghe and Njela (together kusa1251) as dialects of one language (89.8% shared basic vocabulary by her recount, vs Tryon & Hackman's 77.6% that led to the separate ISO code). Davis describes primarily the Hoava dialect and notes Kusaghe variants where they exist; her Kusaghe data come from five weeks in Paradise village (1990); Njela was never visited and is known only from reports. The word-stress rules (sec. 3.4) are stated for the language as a whole with no Kusaghe deviation reported; the only prosodic dialect difference given is phrase-final intonation (sec. 3.5). The catalog already holds hoav1238 coded set by morphology from this same source and section, so a kusa1251 entry would be the same statement applied to a Glottolog-split sister lect -- flag as a potential duplicate-of hoav1238 by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) rather than an independent data point.

tone.quote: The Hoava, Kusaghe and Njela dialects differ in their intonation, a feature often commented on by speakers of Hoava in particular. Both Kusaghe and Njela may lengthen the final stressed syllable of a phrase and sharply lower the pitch on that syllable, followed by a monotone for any remaining unstressed syllables: ... The Njela dialect uses a lower pitch than Kusaghe, and the stressed syllable is greatly lengthened
tone.summary: No lexical tone mentioned anywhere; pitch appears only as Kusaghe/Njela phrase-final intonation (lengthened, lowered final stressed syllable). Word stress described in detail (sec 3.4).
